newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr takes long awaited easing in stride.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr takes long awaited easing in stride.

text.p: The Australian dollar took a long anticipated rate cut in its stride Wednesday even though the exact timing of the move came as something of a surprise.

The Reserve Bank cut its official cash rate 50 basis points to 5.0 percent, the fifth since the easing cycle began a year ago when rates stood at 7.5 percent. The market had been pricing in such a move for more than a month and, after a kneejerk wobble, the dollar quickly recovered its poise.
The resilience was also attributed to expectations this was the last cut in the cycle, although analysts cautioned past experience strongly suggested nothing should be ruled out.
By 12.30 pm (0230 GMT) the dollar had boomeranged to US$0.7457/62 having brielfy dipped to US$0.7395 immediately after the RBA announcement hit dealing screens.
This was a sterling performance given it had finished here Tuesday at US$0.7360/65 and the market had been convinced the bank would not move before its monthly board meeting next week.

Some said it was a growing realisation a cut was discounted which partly prompted the offshore rally. Speculators were very short A$ having sold aggressively since the prior move on May 23, when it had been up at 78 cents, and traders suspected they saw little more downside even if the bank did ease.

Buying from several sources, including a Swiss bank, a U.S. fund and a Canadian corporate, put the squeeze on those short positions and sparked panic stop loss bids when key levels at US$0.7380, US$0.7420 and US$0.7470 were breached.
The currency spiked all the way to 75 cents before caution reasserted itself and it opened this morning around US$0.7450.
Where it went now depended largely on whether today's move really was the last in the easing cycle, as most analysts wwere predicting.
"We expect 5.00 percent to be the floor for cash rates," said Andrew Pease, senior economist at Nomura Research.

Pease saw a number of reasons why the bank would not move again. One was the risk of protracted dollar weakness which would threaten to undo much of the good work done on bringing inflation down. Another was that there was a lot of monetary policy stimulus already in the pipeline with the cash rate having been cut by 250 basis poits in a year.

And there were signs economic activity was gathering pace with business surveys finding rising confidence and anecdotal evidence of stronger retail spending. This should feed into higher employment, long the missing piece of the recovery, which Pease expected to surprise on the upside in the second half.
"The exceptionally good near-term outlook for inflation is likely to keep the RBA under pressure to consider another easing during the next six months," said Pease.
"But we can only imagine the bank taking rates below five percent if economic activity surprises on the downside over the remainder of 1997."

The futures market seemed of much the same mind although with the December 90 bank bill contract at 95.09 -- implying a rate of 4.91 percent -- suggested an easing bias lingered. After all, economic growth had disappointed for much of the year so far while inflation had improved beyond all expectations.
Data on the housing sector today, for instance, proved softer than expected with building approvals falling 4.5 percent against forecasts of a 1.5 percent dip.
Drawing conclusions from this was difficult since May had been boosted by the Olympic Village development, but the trend did turn negative for the first time in more than a year.

The figures illustrated the risks involved in ruling out another easing particularly if upcoming labour reports also disappointed. Employment has long been the missing piece of the recovery picture and a soft July result, which is due next Thursday, would have the market pondering about policy again.
For now though, dealers felt the assumption of steady policy should see the dollar probe higher short term and looked for a test of the US$0.7520/7550 resistance band by the end of the week.
A drop below 74 cents at any time would suggest the rally was a false one and further consolidation was on the cards.

The currency was broadly firmer on the crosses helped by heavy short covering on AUD/yen positions which lifted it to 88.20/30 yen from 86.58/68 late Tuesday. It also leapt to 5-1/2 year highs on the mark around 1.3760 and surged to 58.3 in trade weighted terms from 57.6. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
